storylines.label: Inkling Mini
storylines.latest_title: Show HN: Rust agent with an Inkling 2 Mini inference engine for Apple Silicon

editorial.tldr: Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on Nov 20: a looped multimodal MoE with about 26B total parameters, roughly 3B active per token, and a 1M-token context. vLLM shipped day-0 serving on Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark the same day, with a Docker image.
editorial.whats_new: Five days after launch, an agent-driven tuning run pushed single-user decode on one RTX PRO 6000 from 136 to 190.6 tok/s, and a Rust engine now serves the model on Apple silicon behind an OpenAI-compatible API.
editorial.why_it_matters: A 26B MoE with about 3B active parameters and 1M context now has serving paths on datacenter GPUs, one workstation card and Macs, so local coding-agent backends no longer need a hosted API.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you run a local coding-agent backend, benchmark Inkling 2 Mini with the vLLM Docker image on your own hardware before adopting the community tuning numbers.

status.detail: Open-weight release with vLLM support at launch; community tuning and non-CUDA runtimes followed within a week.

storylines.label: Inference GPU
storylines.latest_title: The model inside the server: Network design for inference on a few GPU nodes

editorial.tldr: This is a loose topic cluster about running inference on GPUs, not one event. Its main thread is AWS adding managed ways to share one GPU: NVIDIA MIG partitions for SageMaker endpoints on Nov 6, then Lambda GPU functions with up to 48 concurrent invocations per model on Nov 22.
editorial.whats_new: An APNIC design guide for self-hosted inference on a few GPU nodes, built on a 4-server, 8-GPU vLLM setup running Llama 3.3 70B, argues that request handling and session count matter more than GPU-to-GPU bandwidth.
editorial.why_it_matters: Whether you rent shared GPUs from AWS or run a few nodes yourself, utilization now depends on how requests are batched and routed more than on raw interconnect speed.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before buying faster interconnect for a small self-hosted cluster, load-test request concurrency and session counts on vLLM; for bursty small models, benchmark SageMaker MIG and Lambda GPU first.

storylines.label: Inference Server
storylines.latest_title: The model inside the server: Network design for inference on a few GPU nodes

editorial.tldr: This is a loose thread of three unrelated pieces on running your own LLM inference server, not one developing event. It began with a hobbyist Qwen trainer-plus-server on Show HN (Nov 12) and an arXiv paper on Superfluid, a local server that distributes inference across devices (Nov 13).
editorial.whats_new: An APNIC post works through a 4-server, 8-GPU vLLM deployment of Llama 3.3 70B and argues request handling and session count, not GPU-to-GPU bandwidth, decide network design at that scale.
editorial.why_it_matters: For small self-hosted inference fleets, the bottleneck claim shifts sizing effort from interconnect spend toward request routing and concurrency limits.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before buying faster interconnect for a 2–4 node inference cluster, load-test your real concurrent session count and request mix against the current network first.

editorial.tldr: This is a loose thread of unrelated arXiv technical reports, not one developing event. It opened Nov 9 with MNN-Pocket-0.3B, a 300M on-device model, then added sparse MoE models: the Clover diffusion LM (35B total, 3B active) and Beam (501.3B total, 23.4B active, 1M-token context).
editorial.whats_new: SAG-Mem-1.0's report (Nov 24) describes a conversational memory framework that stores raw dialogue chunks behind a lexical index with no LLM processing, reporting 83.08 on LoCoMo and 80.20 on LongMemEval.
editorial.why_it_matters: The reports span different serving shapes: sub-1B INT4 on-device models, sparse MoE models up to 501B, and a memory layer that skips LLM calls at write time, each with its own runtime and cost profile.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat these as research reads. If you run agent memory, benchmark SAG-Mem's no-LLM chunk-and-index approach against your summarization pipeline on LoCoMo or LongMemEval before paying for write-time LLM calls.

storylines.label: Speculative Decoding
storylines.latest_title: Draft Calibration for Speculative Decoding: Accelerating LLM Serving by Matching Draft and Target Distributions

editorial.tldr: This thread was regrouped around speculative decoding, so it is now a run of preprints on drafting tokens cheaply and verifying them in one target pass. Nov 7-10 papers trained drafters directly on acceptance length and built block-diffusion draft trees, then Nov 13-20 work moved into serving: invalidated KV caches, looped models and grammar-constrained outputs.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 24: three papers attack the drafter itself: temperature-scaling the draft model lifts acceptance length up to ~10% at almost no cost, LEGOSpec trains swappable draft parts under matched conditions, and Pando reports 5.3x on an edge device.
editorial.why_it_matters: Speculative decoding is a serving-side lever on decode latency and cost that leaves the target model's outputs unchanged, and this month's papers tune the parts an inference team actually owns: the drafter, the draft-tree shape, the KV cache and structured-output paths.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you run speculative decoding, log acceptance length per route before changing anything, then try the cheapest lever first: temperature-scale your existing drafter on your own traffic, and for JSON or tool-call endpoints check whether grammar-forced tokens can fill draft rows.

storylines.label: Harness Performance
storylines.latest_title: Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance

editorial.tldr: Hugging Face opened the thread on Nov 20 by training a LoRA adapter that fits a model to its harness, raising Qwen3.8-27B's Terminal-Bench 2.1 pass@1 from 39% to 55% on half the tokens. On Nov 23 Jcode, an open-source Rust harness, shifted the lever to running parallel agents on one repo with a server that coordinates file changes.
editorial.whats_new: Delegent, an arXiv harness built on Claude Code, keeps a frontier model in charge and hands easy subtasks to a small local model, reporting 67% lower frontier cost on long-horizon coding and 59% on agentic search.
editorial.why_it_matters: Three separate teams treat the harness, not the model, as the tuning surface for agent cost and pass rate: adapter training, parallel orchestration, and frontier-to-local delegation.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before switching models to cut agent cost, benchmark harness changes on your own tasks: log frontier-token spend per subtask and test routing the cheap ones to a local model.

status.detail: Each result is self-reported by its authors on its own benchmark; no item yet compares the three approaches on a shared task.

storylines.label: Inference Engines
storylines.latest_title: Can agents write inference engines from scratch in 12 hours and beat vLLM?

editorial.tldr: This is a loose theme thread, not one event: three unrelated sources over two weeks treated the inference engine itself as the object of work. It opened with EngineAgent, a paper on using agents to port new LLM architectures into on-device engines, and a Nov 22 paper on stripping backdoor activations at inference time.
editorial.whats_new: Humanity's Last System (HLS), an open benchmark, gives coding agents live GPU sandboxes for up to 36 hours to build inference servers that are verified and scored for speed against vLLM-style baselines.
editorial.why_it_matters: Agent-written serving code is moving from research prototype to scored benchmark, so the speed claims around custom inference engines will soon come with a public yardstick against vLLM.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat agent-built inference servers as unproven until HLS publishes verified scores; keep vLLM as the serving baseline and rerun your own latency evals before swapping engines.

storylines.label: Vllm Inference
storylines.latest_title: Can agents write inference engines from scratch in 12 hours and beat vLLM?

editorial.tldr: This is a theme thread, not one event: three separate items treat vLLM as the default open serving stack. It opened with Warmctl, a Show HN tool for faster vLLM cold starts, then vLLM shipped day-0 support for Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview through a plugin.
editorial.whats_new: Humanity's Last System (HLS), an open benchmark, gives coding agents live GPU sandboxes for up to 36 hours to build inference servers, then verifies them and scores their speed against vLLM-style baselines.
editorial.why_it_matters: vLLM is now the reference point for serving: new models ship as vLLM plugins, tools patch its cold starts, and agent benchmarks measure themselves against it.
editorial.take_for_builders: For ERNIE 5.5 Flash, pin vllm==0.32.0 with the vllm-ERNIE plugin. Treat HLS results as research until verified scores beat your own vLLM baseline on your models.

storylines.label: Multi-agent Systems
storylines.latest_title: Towards Realistic Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification for LLM-Based Recommender Systems

editorial.tldr: This is a theme thread, not one event: three weeks of mostly arXiv work on what breaks when LLM agents run as a team, starting with KV-cache memory cost and workflow orchestration. It then split into two tracks: securing agents against malicious peers and data leaks, and tracing which agent caused a failure.
editorial.whats_new: LatentLens (Nov 23) reports that a latent agent-to-agent interface often fails to improve accuracy and can degrade it across seven benchmarks, the same day REPA modeled how one agent's local errors cascade into system failure.
editorial.why_it_matters: Multi-agent reliability now has concrete failure models (error propagation, malicious feedback during replanning, cross-agent data leaks), so a single end-to-end success rate no longer tells you why your agent team fails.
editorial.take_for_builders: Log each agent's messages and intermediate outputs per step in your multi-agent runs, because failure attribution and error-propagation methods like CoLFA and REPA need per-agent traces, not just the final answer.

storylines.label: Uncertainty Quantification
storylines.latest_title: Towards Realistic Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification for LLM-Based Recommender Systems

editorial.tldr: On Nov 13 an arXiv paper proposed ensemble-of-ensembles uncertainty estimates for black-box LLMs that split prompt ambiguity from knowledge gaps. A Nov 18 paper moved the question to evaluation, estimating benchmark performance from at most 31 revealed outcomes with a Beta prior.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 24 benchmark tested eight uncertainty signals as monitors of LLM recommender rankings on four datasets and found the method ranking changes when the LLM backbone changes.
editorial.why_it_matters: A confidence signal tuned on one model may not carry over when you swap the backbone, so uncertainty-based routing, abstention, and monitoring need per-model validation.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you gate, route, or abstain on an uncertainty score, re-check its calibration on your eval set every time you change the underlying model.

storylines.label: Weight-Space Programming
storylines.latest_title: Can a Frontier LLM Repair a Quantized Network by Tool-Free Weight-Space Programming?

editorial.tldr: An MIT report that a frontier LLM can write and read small neural network weights in one reply set off mid-November follow-ups: an open-source instruction set (W-ISA), a game-agent compilation paper, an independent replication, and value-edit and CLIP papers. On Nov 24, MBZUAI showed a Claude Opus 5.5-written transformer solving all of its test mazes for $19.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 24 arXiv paper reports Claude-family models, given only a 20k-parameter CIFAR-10 CNN's weights as text and no tools or data, repaired its 4-bit version from 60.4% to 77.95% accuracy, against 81.4% for the float network.
editorial.why_it_matters: Weight-writing now covers repair as well as construction: an LLM reading raw weights recovered most of a quantization loss without data, and the same method can change a model's behavior with no training trail.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat LLM-written weights as a research option for small, verifiable models only; keep your standard quantization pipeline. Add checkpoint hashing and behavior regression evals now, since direct weight edits leave no training trail.

storylines.label: Cache Serving
storylines.latest_title: LoomKV: Lossless KV Cache Compression from GPU Memory to SSD for LLM Serving

editorial.tldr: This is a theme thread, not one event: 13 items from Nov 6 to Nov 24 that each cut LLM serving cost at a different layer, mostly arXiv papers plus Google's XLA Serving Engine launch and an AWS case study. Through Nov 19 the KV cache was the most-attacked target, ending with RoCoKV and TideCache.
editorial.whats_new: LoomKV (Nov 24) compresses the KV cache losslessly from GPU memory down to SSD on an unmodified serving engine, storing BF16 KV at 0.71x raw size and reporting 2.7-3.6x raw goodput on the AgentX trace.
editorial.why_it_matters: KV-cache memory is the dominant serving bottleneck in this thread (7 of 13 items), and LoomKV is the first entry that claims lossless savings without engine changes, so cache tiering may become a drop-in layer rather than a fork.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you offload KV cache with LMCache or similar, measure goodput as the working set crosses your LRU capacity before adding GPUs; that cliff is where LoomKV claims its gains.
